--- title: "Wednesday" description: "Containers and Nextflow workflows" date: "2026-09-16" categories: [containers, Apptainer, Nextflow, RNA-seq, Salmon] engine: knitr --- ## What we did today First we learned about **containers** and ran our QC tools inside them with **Apptainer**. Then we learned the basics of the workflow manager **Nextflow** and used it to build a small **RNA-seq workflow** (index → quantify → QC → report). ## Part 1: Containers ### What is a container? A Pixi environment packs the *tools*. A **container** goes one step further: it packs the tools **and a whole operating system** into a single file, called an **image**. Because the operating system travels with it, a container runs the same way on my laptop, on a colleague's computer and on a cluster. Images do not change once they are built, so they stay stable over time. Popular container programs are Docker, Podman and **Apptainer** (earlier called *Singularity*). On shared servers like HPC2N, Apptainer is the right choice. ### Getting an image Two good places to find images: - **[Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com)**: images that people have uploaded. The [biocontainers](https://hub.docker.com/u/biocontainers) profile has many well-built bioinformatics tools. - **[Seqera Containers](https://seqera.io/containers/)**: builds an image on request from conda-forge/bioconda packages, and can put several tools into one image. Choose **Singularity** as the format. #we used this to get containers for Salmon, FastQC and MultiQC. ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # from Seqera (note the oras:// prefix) apptainer pull vcftools_0.1.17.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/vcftools:0.1.17--b541aa8d9f9213f9 ``` ::: The first name (`vcftools_0.1.17.sif`) is what the file is called on my computer. Putting the tool name **and version** in it makes it clear what is inside. ### Using a container ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # run one command inside the container ("from the outside") apptainer exec vcftools_0.1.17.sif vcftools --version # open a shell inside the container ("from the inside"), type exit to leave apptainer shell vcftools_0.1.17.sif # make a folder from outside visible inside the container with -B outside:inside apptainer exec -B ../data:/rawdata fastqc_0.12.1.sif ls /rawdata ``` ::: `exec` vs `run`: - `apptainer exec` runs **the command I give it**. This is what I use most. - `apptainer run` first runs the container's built-in **runscript** (its default action). ### Building my own container If nobody has made an image for a tool, I can build one from a **definition file**. The course example was a cow that tells the date: ```{.default filename="lolcow.def"} Bootstrap: docker From: ubuntu:22.04 %post apt-get -y update apt-get -y install cowsay lolcat fortune %environment export LC_ALL=C export PATH=/usr/games:$PATH %runscript date | cowsay | lolcat ``` - `From:` which operating system to start from - `%post` commands that install things - `%environment` settings available when the container runs - `%runscript` what `apptainer run` does ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} apptainer build lolcow.sif lolcow.def apptainer run lolcow.sif ``` ::: ### QC with containers We repeated Tuesday's QC, but with FastQC and MultiQC from containers instead of the Pixi environment. The only change in the SLURM script is the command line: ```{.bash filename="scripts/fastqc_container.sh"} #! /bin/bash -l #SBATCH -A #SBATCH -t 30:00 #SBATCH -n 1 apptainer exec ../containers/fastqc_0.12.1.sif fastqc -o ../fastqc --noextract ../data/*fastq.gz ``` MultiQC from the outside and from the inside: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # outside apptainer exec containers/multiqc.sif multiqc fastqc -o multiqc # inside apptainer shell containers/multiqc.sif multiqc fastqc -o multiqc exit ``` ::: ## Part 2: Nextflow basics ### Why a workflow manager? Nextflow: - connects the steps so the output of one becomes the input of the next, - runs independent tasks **in parallel**, - remembers what already finished, so I can **resume** after an error, - separates **what** to run (the workflow) from **where** to run it (laptop, cluster, cloud). This is called *execution abstraction*. ### The building blocks - **process**: one step, e.g. "run FastQC". It has `input`, `output` and a `script`. - **channel**: a queue that carries data from one process to the next. - **workflow**: the part that connects processes and channels. - **executor**: where the tasks run (`local` or `slurm`). ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A(["greeting_ch
'Hello world!'"]) --> B["SPLITLETTERS"] B --> C(["chunk_aa, chunk_ab"]) C -->|flatten| D["CONVERTTOUPPER"] D --> E(["HELLO
WORLD!"]) ``` ### Setting up ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} screen -S nextflow cp -r /path/to/repbio26/common_data/nf-training . cd nf-training pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda pixi add nextflow ``` ::: ### hello.nf ```{.groovy filename="hello.nf"} #!/usr/bin/env nextflow params.greeting = 'Hello world!' // a parameter I can change from the command line process SPLITLETTERS { input: val x // a value output: path 'chunk_*' // files starting with chunk_ script: """ printf '$x' | split -b 6 - chunk_ """ } process CONVERTTOUPPER { input: path y output: stdout // whatever is printed script: """ cat $y | tr '[a-z]' '[A-Z]' """ } workflow { greeting_ch = Channel.of(params.greeting) letters_ch = SPLITLETTERS(greeting_ch) results_ch = CONVERTTOUPPER(letters_ch.flatten()) // flatten: one task per chunk results_ch.view{ it } } ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} pixi run nextflow run hello.nf ``` ::: Output: ``` executor > local (3) [96/fd5f07] SPLITLETTERS (1) [100%] 1 of 1 ✔ [7e/dad424] CONVERTTOUPPER (2) [100%] 2 of 2 ✔ HELLO WORLD! ``` The codes like `96/fd5f07` are the start of the folder in `work/` where that task ran. It is useful for debugging. `HELLO` and `WORLD!` can come in any order because the two tasks run in parallel. ### Resume and parameters ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # after changing a process: only the changed part is re-run, the rest comes from the cache pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume # change a parameter from the command line (two dashes = pipeline parameter) pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume --greeting 'Bonjour le monde!' ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## One dash or two? `-resume` has **one** dash, so it is an option for Nextflow itself. `--greeting` has **two** dashes, so it is a parameter of *my* pipeline. ::: Settings can come from many places. The most important ones, from strongest to weakest: command line (`--param`) → `-params-file` → `-c my.config` → `nextflow.config` in the current folder → values in the script. ### Cleaning up The `work/` folder grows fast. ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} pixi run nextflow log # list previous runs in this folder pixi run nextflow clean -f # remove work files pixi run nextflow clean -before -f ``` ::: ## Part 3: A simple RNA-seq workflow with Nextflow We built this workflow step by step in `script1.nf` to `script7.nf`: ```{mermaid} flowchart TD T([transcriptome.fa]) --> IDX["INDEX
salmon index"] R([paired-end reads]) -->|fromFilePairs| RP([read pairs per sample]) IDX --> Q["QUANTIFICATION
salmon quant"] RP --> Q RP --> FQ["FASTQC"] Q --> M["MULTIQC"] FQ --> M M --> REP([multiqc_report.html]) ``` - **INDEX**: Salmon turns the transcriptome into a searchable index. This is done once. - **QUANTIFICATION**: for each sample, Salmon estimates how much of each transcript is present. - **FASTQC**: checks read quality. It runs *at the same time* as quantification, because neither needs the other. - **MULTIQC**: waits for everything and makes one report. ### Running on the cluster: `nextflow.config` Running on the login node is not allowed on a cluster, so we told Nextflow to send every task to SLURM. This file is read automatically when it is in the folder where I run Nextflow: ```{.groovy filename="nextflow.config"} process { executor = "slurm" time = '2.h' // default time for every process cpus = 4 withName: 'INDEX' { // settings only for the INDEX process time = 15.m cpus = 2 } withName: 'QUANTIFICATION' { time = 30.m cpus = 2 } } resume = true // always resume, no need to type -resume singularity.enabled = true executor { account = '' } ``` ### Channels of read pairs Salmon needs both files of a pair together. `fromFilePairs` groups them by sample name. The `{1,2}` marks the part of the file name that differs: ```{.groovy} read_pairs_ch = channel.fromFilePairs(params.reads) read_pairs_ch.view() // [gut, [/.../gut_1.fq, /.../gut_2.fq]] <- a tuple: sample ID + list of two files ``` ### The complete workflow This is what my final script looked like. Each process gets its tool from a container, which is more reproducible than installing the tools in the environment: ```{.groovy filename="script7.nf"} #!/usr/bin/env nextflow params.reads = "$projectDir/data/ggal/gut_{1,2}.fq" params.transcriptome_file = "$projectDir/data/ggal/transcriptome.fa" params.outdir = "results" workflow { read_pairs_ch = channel.fromFilePairs(params.reads, checkIfExists: true) index_ch = INDEX(file(params.transcriptome_file, checkIfExists: true)) quant_ch = QUANTIFICATION(index_ch, read_pairs_ch) fastqc_ch = FASTQC(read_pairs_ch) // mix: put both channels together; collect: wait for all and pass them as ONE item MULTIQC(quant_ch.mix(fastqc_ch).collect()) } process INDEX { container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7' input: path transcriptome output: path 'salmon_index' script: """ salmon index --threads $task.cpus -t $transcriptome -i salmon_index """ } process QUANTIFICATION { tag "Salmon on $sample_id" container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7' publishDir "$params.outdir/salmon", mode: 'copy' input: path salmon_index tuple val(sample_id), path(reads) output: path "$sample_id" script: """ salmon quant --threads $task.cpus --libType=U -i $salmon_index -1 ${reads[0]} -2 ${reads[1]} -o $sample_id """ } process FASTQC { tag "FastQC on $sample_id" container '' input: tuple val(sample_id), path(reads) output: path "fastqc_${sample_id}_logs" script: """ mkdir fastqc_${sample_id}_logs fastqc -o fastqc_${sample_id}_logs -f fastq -q ${reads} """ } process MULTIQC { container '' publishDir "$params.outdir/multiqc", mode: 'copy' input: path '*' output: path 'multiqc_report.html' script: """ multiqc . """ } ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code} # run on all three samples (gut, liver, lung) pixi run nextflow run script7.nf --reads 'data/ggal/*_{1,2}.fq' ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## `publishDir` and `mode: 'copy'` By default, `publishDir` only makes *links* to files inside `work/`. If I clean `work/`, the results disappear. `mode: 'copy'` makes real copies that survive the cleanup. ::: ## Cheat sheet | I want to... | Command | |---|---| | download an image | `apptainer pull .sif docker://...` or `oras://...` | | run a tool in a container | `apptainer exec .sif ` | | work inside a container | `apptainer shell .sif` | | make a folder visible inside | `-B outside/path:inside/path` | | build an image | `apptainer build .sif .def` | | run a Nextflow script | `pixi run nextflow run script.nf` | | continue where it stopped | add `-resume` | | change a parameter | add `--param_name value` | | see previous runs / clean up | `nextflow log` / `nextflow clean -f` | ## Notes {#notes}
